analysis.one_liner: Abolishes the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, the federal watchdog over consumer finance.
analysis.headline: The bill to eliminate the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau drew only 6 of 223 House Republicans as cosponsors and has received no action since its February referral to committee.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would repeal the 2010 law that created the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, abolishing the federal agency that handles consumer complaints and polices abusive practices in mortgages, credit cards, debt collection, and credit reporting. It would also restore the law as it stood before 2010. Since the day it was introduced, it has sat without action in the House Financial Services Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Banks, credit card issuers, payday and installment lenders, debt collectors, and credit reporting agencies. Repealing the Consumer Financial Protection Act would abolish the bureau's authority to write rules, examine companies, and bring enforcement actions against these firms, and would restore the legal framework as it existed before 2010. The bill contains no benefits for consumers.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Consumer Financial Protection Act of 2010 in its entirety, eliminating the bureau's power to write consumer-finance rules, examine firms, and take enforcement actions.
Restores the law as if the 2010 act had never been enacted, meaning the agency and the framework that created it would disappear together.
Ends the bureau's supervision and complaint-handling for firms it covers — the regulated companies would no longer face bureau examinations, penalties, or investigations of consumer complaints.

analysis.who_pays: Consumers who use credit — mortgage holders, credit card users, people with loans in collection, and anyone whose credit file contains errors. They would lose the single federal agency that takes their complaints, writes rules against abusive practices, and returns money to consumers through enforcement.

drawbacks.text: Consumers would lose the one federal agency dedicated to taking their complaints about mortgages, credit cards, debt collection, and credit reporting, and to penalizing firms for abusive practices.
Existing consumer-finance rules would be left without the agency that enforces them, since the bill abolishes the bureau and revives the pre-2010 legal framework.

The good-faith case for the bill: supporters argue the bureau is structurally unaccountable — funded through the Federal Reserve rather than yearly appropriations and run by a single director with broad rulemaking power — and that consumer oversight could instead sit with the existing banking regulators, as it did before 2010.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits in this bill flow entirely to regulated financial firms through reduced oversight and enforcement; the text contains nothing for consumers, who would bear the cost of weaker recourse against abusive lending, collection, and credit-reporting practices. The one honest argument for it — reining in an agency its critics see as unaccountable — is a trade-off, not a consumer benefit, and the bill offers no replacement structure before 2010 rules lapse from active enforcement.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced and nothing has happened to it since.

narrative.text: Representative Byron Donalds introduced the Repeal CFPB Act on February 26, 2025, joined by original cosponsors including Representatives Ogles, Norman, and McCormick.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day and has received no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote.
Only 6 of 223 House Republicans signed on as cosponsors, and no Democrat did.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers, for now: the bill never advanced, so the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and the rules it enforces remain in place. Financial firms gained nothing from this attempt.

for.name: Byron Donalds
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to abolish the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau.

for.name: 6 of 223 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no Democrat or independent signed on.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. French Hill (R-AR)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup; the record shows no committee action after the referral.

against.name: Consumer advocacy organizations
against.what_they_did: Opposed eliminating the bureau, which they view as the main federal protector of consumers in lending and debt collection.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor is Republican — 6 of 223 House Republicans, with no Democrat or independent support — and no vote was ever taken in either chamber.

industries.note: Abolishing the bureau would end its supervision, examinations, and enforcement against banks and card issuers, including its fee and lending-practice rules. Their gain in reduced oversight is consumers' loss of protection.
The bureau has been the main federal regulator policing payday and installment lending; repeal would remove that oversight entirely.

industries.industry: Debt collectors and credit reporting agencies
industries.note: These industries face heavy bureau rulemaking and enforcement over collection practices and credit-file accuracy; with the bureau gone, federal policing of those practices would end.

analysis.trajectory: Unlikely to advance. The bill has only 6 cosponsors, no Democratic support, and no committee action since its February referral; standalone repeal bills of this kind have historically died in committee without a floor vote. Its realistic path is remaining dormant unless its provisions are attached to a broader financial deregulation package.
